"The positivity to natural affection displayed by this father for his son, as described, reflects the goodness of God, who is more clement to sinful man if he repents and despises himself, than any father to his son, however tenderly he may love him." This statement is from Method of True Theology, a preface to the first edition of his New Testament.

Theological Writings can be divided into four parallel and complementary lines of work:
1. Establishing and critical elucidation of biblical texts.
2. Editions of great patristic commentators.
3. Exegetical works, where the results of the first two researches are applied.
4. Methodological works, which serve as a preface to the various other studies and are nourished by them in return.

Recent studies question the analysis of E and J as strictly separate. Coats argues that Abraham's obedience to God's command necessitates praise and blessing, which he only receives in the second angelic speech. This has led many to suggest that the author responsible for the interpolation of the second angelic appearance has also left his mark on the original account (v. 1–13, 19). More recently, it has been suggested that these traces are in fact the first angelic appearance (v. ).

Erasmus criticizes the doctrines and morals of the Reformers, stating that they are not content to retrench abuses in prayers, fasts, and Masses, but must abolish them entirely. He complains that the 'Evangelical' generation shows no less indulgence to luxury, lust, or avarice than those they detest. He questions whether anyone has been reclaimed from drunkenness or other vices by the Gospel.
